params.notes: Hours worked = time the employee is suffered or permitted to work; the Portal-to-Portal Act excludes ordinary commuting and activities preliminary or postliminary to the principal activity (incl. security screening, Integrity Staffing v. Busk 2014); 29 CFR 785.47 lets insubstantial, irregular minutes be disregarded

result.summary: Under the FLSA all time an employee is suffered or permitted to work is paid, except ordinary commuting and preliminary or postliminary activities excluded by the Portal-to-Portal Act; a de minimis exception exists.
Ordinary home-to-work travel is not hours worked, even to different worksites, unless the employee works during the trip.
Travel between job sites during the workday, or from the employer's premises to the first site after reporting, is hours worked.

rules.title: FLSA — Travel Time (Special One Day Assignment)

params.notes: Employer may deduct the normal home-to-work commute time

result.summary: A special one-day assignment in another city is hours worked, less the time of the employee's normal commute.

Overnight travel away from home is hours worked only during the employee's normal working hours (including corresponding hours on non-working days); passenger time outside those hours is unpaid unless work is done.

Riding employer-provided transport from a meeting point to the worksite is not hours worked under the Portal-to-Portal Act unless the travel is itself a principal activity; several states (CA, NY, WA, MD, PA, MA) count it.

params.test: engaged to wait: employee must remain on the premises or so close that the time cannot be used effectively for personal purposes

result.summary: An employee required to stay on or near the premises while on call is working and must be paid.

params.test: waiting to be engaged: employee may leave a contact number and use the time for personal purposes
params.notes: Time actually spent responding to calls is paid

result.summary: An on-call employee who need only leave a contact number and can use the time freely is not working; only time responding to calls is paid.

params.notes: Attendance is not voluntary if required or if the employee is led to believe non-attendance would hurt their job

result.summary: Required training, orientation and meetings are hours worked.

params.exclusion_test: all four: outside regular hours, genuinely voluntary, not directly related to the employee's current job, and no productive work performed
params.notes: Training to acquire a new or additional skill is not 'directly related'; apprenticeship instruction and independent courses are excluded

result.summary: Training is unpaid only when it is outside regular hours, voluntary, not directly related to the current job and involves no productive work; otherwise it is hours worked.

params.notes: Rounding to the nearest 5, 6 or 15 minutes is accepted where it averages out and does not fail to pay for all time actually worked over a period

result.summary: Punches may be rounded to the nearest quarter hour (or smaller increment) if the practice is neutral and does not, over time, fail to pay employees for all hours worked.

rules.title: District of Columbia — Hours Worked Standard

result.summary: District of Columbia follows the federal hours-worked rules; the District defines working time broadly as time the employee is required to be at the place of employment or on duty, applied with federal practice (7 DCMR 999 definitions unverified).

params.notes: Control test (Morillion); no de minimis for regularly recurring minutes (Troester); mandatory on-site security checks are paid (Frlekin v. Apple 2020)

result.summary: California pays for all time the employee is subject to the employer's control, whether or not working; the Portal-to-Portal exclusions and the federal de minimis rule do not apply.

citations.source: Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal.4th 575 (2000)

params.notes: Time worked includes on-premises waiting for assignments; off-site on-call depends on restriction

result.summary: Colorado counts all time performing labor or services for the employer's benefit, including required pre- and post-shift tasks (gear, check-in, security, clean-up) that take more than one minute.

citations.source: CDLE INFO #20: Time Worked That Must Be Paid

result.summary: Connecticut regulations define hours worked (including on-call time the employee cannot use freely) and make travel at the employer's request compensable.
Illinois defines hours worked as all time the employee is required to be on duty or at a prescribed workplace, including travel between worksites and required training, close to federal practice.
Kentucky's hours-worked regulation tracks the federal rules but counts overnight travel that cuts across the workday without the federal passenger-time exclusion.

Maryland counts time the employee is required to be on the premises, on duty or at a prescribed workplace; the Court of Appeals held in 2022 that the Portal-to-Portal exclusions were never adopted, so waiting at and travelling from a prescribed meeting point can be paid time.

citations.source: Amaya v. DGS Construction, LLC, 479 Md. 515 (2022)

result.summary: Massachusetts defines working time to include on-call time the employee cannot use effectively and travel between worksites or from a required reporting point; treble damages apply to unpaid time.
Minnesota counts training, call time, cleaning and waiting time and restricted on-call time as hours worked; rest breaks under 20 minutes may not be deducted.
Montana's hours-worked rules mirror the federal interpretations on waiting, on-call, travel and training time.
Nevada pays for all time the employee is working or under the employer's control, including travel between worksites and employer-required travel, but not the ordinary commute.
New Jersey regulations define hours worked, including restricted on-call time and time waiting at the employer's direction, in line with federal practice.

New York counts time the employee is required to be available for work at a place prescribed by the employer, which reaches mandatory pre-shift logistics and employer-required transit; the citation URL is a placeholder for the Labor Department regulation.
North Dakota's wage order sets out travel, on-call, waiting and training rules that follow the federal interpretations, with state-mandated occupational training excluded.
Oregon's rules define hours worked and specify waiting, sleeping, preparatory, training and travel time; they follow federal structure but courts have read Oregon law to bar time rounding.

Pennsylvania's Minimum Wage Act defines hours worked to include time at the employer's direction on or off premises and travel as part of duties; the Supreme Court held in 2021 that the Portal-to-Portal exclusions and de minimis rule do not apply, so security screening time is paid.

params.notes: Port of Tacoma v. Sacks (Wash. Ct. App. 2021) and Anderson v. DSHS: all work-related travel compensable

result.summary: Washington counts all time the employee is authorized or required to be on duty on the premises or at a prescribed workplace; unlike federal law all out-of-town travel is paid.

citations.source: L&I Administrative Policy ES.C.2, Hours Worked (rev. 2021-07-19)

result.summary: Wisconsin adopts most federal hours-worked interpretations but counts all travel time, including passenger time on overnight trips outside normal hours.

params.notes: Optional employer-provided transport the employee may decline is not

result.summary: Time riding employer-required transport (e.g. a mandatory bus from a meeting point) is hours worked because the employee is under the employer's control.

citations.source: Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal.4th 575 (2000)

params.notes: Commute in an employer vehicle with restrictions on personal use may be compensable

result.summary: An ordinary commute the employee controls is not hours worked; it becomes paid if the employer requires a particular route, vehicle or reporting point.

citations.source: Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal.4th 575 (2000)
DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual §46 (travel time)

result.summary: All time spent travelling on employer-required out-of-town trips is hours worked, including as a passenger outside normal hours, less the normal commute; a lower agreed travel rate (at least minimum wage) may be set in advance.

citations.source: DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual §46 (travel time)

result.summary: Travel between worksites during the day is hours worked.

citations.source: DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual §46 (travel time)

params.test: control test: degree of restriction on the employee's activities (Mendiola)
params.notes: Sleep time may be excluded only where a wage order expressly allows it

result.summary: On-call time on the employer's premises or under its control is hours worked, including sleep time on 24-hour shifts, because the employee cannot use it for their own purposes.

citations.source: Mendiola v. CPS Security Solutions, Inc., 60 Cal.4th 833 (2015)

result.summary: Required training, orientation and meetings are hours worked and the employer must bear their cost; a training rate lower than the regular rate (at least minimum wage) may be set in advance.

params.notes: See's Candy (2012) allowed neutral rounding; Camp v. Home Depot review pending at the Supreme Court

result.summary: Neutral rounding survives only where the system does not capture exact time; meal-period punches may never be rounded (Donohue) and an employer that records exact punches must pay to the minute (Camp, Woodworth), so pay-to-the-minute is the safe practice.

citations.source: Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC, 11 Cal.5th 58 (2021)
Camp v. Home Depot U.S.A., Inc., 84 Cal.App.5th 638 (2022), review granted

result.summary: All out-of-town travel required for work is hours worked in Washington, including travel to the airport and passenger time outside normal hours; only free time at the destination is unpaid.

Port of Tacoma v. Sacks, 19 Wn. App. 2d 295 (2021)

result.summary: Travel between worksites during the day, and from a required reporting point to the first site, is hours worked.

result.summary: Neutral rounding to the nearest quarter hour is accepted for shift punches but not for meal or rest periods; a policy that favours the employer in practice is unlawful (Bennett v. Providence, 2025).

rules.title: Oregon — Travel Time (Special One Day Assignment)

result.summary: A one-day assignment to a site more than 30 miles from the regular workplace is hours worked; call-backs within the 30-mile radius count only the time beyond the normal commute.
Travel between job sites during the workday, or from a required reporting location to the site, is hours worked.

params.notes: Required certification training outside regular hours is not compensable (subsection 7)

result.summary: Training and meetings are hours worked unless outside regular hours, voluntary, not directly job-related and without productive work; state-mandated certification training outside hours is excluded.
Oregon law has been held not to permit time rounding; BOLI advises employers who round to true up unpaid minutes each pay period or round only in the employee's favour.

citations.source: Eisele v. Home Depot U.S.A., Inc., 643 F. Supp. 3d 1166 (D. Or. 2022)

result.summary: Travel for the employer's benefit, such as driving between appointments or sites, is time worked.

result.summary: Required training and meetings are hours worked; unpaid only if outside hours, voluntary, not job-related and without productive work.

rules.title: New York — Travel Time (Employer Mandated Transport)

result.summary: Time an employee is required to be available for work at a place the employer prescribes, including mandatory transit from a reporting point, is hours worked.
Travel between worksites during the workday is hours worked.
Travel between worksites, and travel from a location the employee must report to before going to a worksite, is working time; related transportation expenses must be reimbursed.
On-call time is working time when the employee cannot use it effectively for their own purposes; leaving a number and being free to go is not.
Travel between worksites and travel the employer requires beyond the normal commute is hours worked.
Travel between worksites during the workday is hours worked.
An employee required to stay on or so near the premises that the time cannot be used for personal purposes is working while on call.
Training time is hours worked.
On-call employees required to remain on the premises or so close they cannot use the time freely are working.
All travel time on an overnight trip for the employer is hours worked; Wisconsin does not apply the federal passenger-time exclusion.
Overnight travel that cuts across the workday is hours worked; Kentucky states no exception for passenger time outside normal hours (encoding approximate; verify against the regulation text).
Travel between worksites and travel the employer requires is hours worked; the ordinary commute is not.
North Carolina accepts the federal 7-minute rule: with quarter-hour rounding, 1-7 minutes round down and 8-14 round up.
The New York Labor Department follows the federal rounding regulation: neutral rounding to the nearest quarter hour is permitted.
Texas applies the federal standard: neutral rounding to the nearest quarter hour is permitted.
